extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, stakeholders, and organizations submitting comments on U.S. federal regulations (notice-and-comment rulemaking)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and submitting effective public comments on proposed U.S. federal regulations, including what to include, how to structure analysis, legal/economic evaluation criteria, and the mechanics of finding and filing comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document identification at top of comment
rubrics_metrics.description: At the top of your comment, identify the document you are commenting on by its docket number, subject heading, federal register date and page number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential for the agency to associate your submission with the correct rulemaking; put this information at the very top of the comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: state interest and credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an introduction where you explain why you are interested in the regulation, highlight any credentials or experience that may distinguish your comment from others, and whether you are commenting on your own behalf, on the behalf of another organization, or are endorsing or joining with another comment or commenter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explaining the commentator's stake and expertise helps establish relevance and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background: identify issues and list recommendations upfront
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a background where you clearly identify the issues within the regulatory action on which you are commenting, and list your recommendations upfront.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If commenting on particular words/phrases or specific questions, state this clearly and provide page, column, and paragraph citation from the Federal Register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis: detailed argument and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an analysis section which lays out your detailed argument and evidence to support your recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support assertions with data, logic, and cited evidence so the agency can assess and respond; this is the core of persuasive commenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion: recap argument and restate recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: End with a conclusion which recaps your main argument and lists your recommendations again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concise summary reinforces the main points for agency reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite all information and research relied on
rubrics_metrics.description: Your comment should include citations for all information and research you relied on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide formatted citations (chapter 5 offers tips). Cite relevant research, data, or analysis and explain why it is relevant to costs/benefits or other impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide information directly relevant to analyzing the rule and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comments provide information directly relevant to analyzing the rule and its effects rather than merely stating support or opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal perspective is valuable when it shows unique situations, impacts on individual behavior, or third-party value judgments, but must connect to analysis of the rule’s effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to in-notice prompts and agency questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay special attention to any in-notice prompts, such as questions or requests for data or evidence, within the proposed rule and respond to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prompts indicate areas the agency considers important and will attract reliable attention from reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether agency is required to regulate
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the agency is required to regulate: (1) a law requires it, (2) interpretation of a law is necessary, or (3) a compelling public need exists (market failure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue whether rulemaking is legally and practically necessary; this affects the legitimacy of the regulatory action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide rigorous analysis of necessity, costs, benefits, and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Your goal is to provide rigorous information regarding whether rulemaking is necessary, the costs and benefits of the proposed rules, and the benefits of other policy alternatives (including maintaining the status quo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you believe the rule fails to maximize net benefits, draw on expertise, research, or evidence to show flaws, undervalued costs/benefits, or propose changes that would increase net benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess rule by agency best-practice standards (e.g., Circular A-4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the rule by the standards to which agency officials are held (for example, Circular A-4 for regulatory analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can demonstrate the agency failed to follow its own analytic procedures and guidance, your comment will be more persuasive and potentially legally significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the problem the regulation intends to address
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the problem the regulation intends to address: why is the regulation needed, what problem is the agency trying to address, and whether private markets or government institutions are currently addressing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must explain how the regulation will address the problem; your comment should evaluate that explanation and show gaps or inaccuracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use best available scientific, technical, and economic information
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether agency regulations are based on the best available scientific, technical, economic, and other information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists, economists, and technical experts can improve rules by lending expert opinion, citing published reports, or providing relevant data or evidence regarding effects or need for the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether costs are justified by benefits (cost-effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the costs of the intended regulation are justified by its benefits and whether the regulation is designed in a cost-effective manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include analysis of innovation incentives, consistency, predictability, enforcement and compliance costs, flexibility, distributive impacts, and equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require reproducible cost/benefit estimates and transparent methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators must explain how they got their estimates of costs and benefits in sufficient detail to allow reproduction; commenters should evaluate and challenge estimation methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask for or provide transparent assumptions, data sources, and methodologies; when monetization is difficult, describe impacts qualitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest and evaluate regulatory alternatives (including baseline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggest alternatives to the proposed regulation (including the baseline of no new regulation) and evaluate how they compare on outcomes and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show if the agency can achieve the same outcomes at lower cost or with lower burden; agencies are required to select approaches that maximize net benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform distributional analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider who bears the costs of a rule and who enjoys its benefits; describe distributional impacts and economic transfers, monetizing where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law requires agencies to consider distributional effects; a rule may be invalid if it disproportionately impacts a group or individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check whether existing regulations created the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether existing agency regulations have created or contributed to the problem the proposed rule seeks to fix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If existing regulations are the source of the problem, recommend repeal or modification rather than a new regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate agency theoretical framework and behavioral assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider agencies' theoretical framework: they should provide a coherent theory, consistent with economic behavior, explaining why a problem exists and how the regulation will solve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain flaws in the underlying theory and the implications for outcomes; identify incorrect behavioral assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess legality, statutory authority, and consistency with other regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the legality and necessity of the rule: regulations should be based on legislation, be unique in what they achieve, and be consistent and compatible with other regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out statutory gaps, overreach, or conflicts with existing regulatory frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify potential 'arbitrary and capricious' defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight defects that courts have found arbitrary and capricious, such as contradicting expert record evidence without explanation; failing to provide any coherent explanation; failing to consider circumstances warranting different treatment; reaching conclusions that contradict the record; failing to consider relevant factors; issuing rules based on political compromise rather than reasoned science; deferring excessively to private parties; using models inconsistent with underlying data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing these defects in your comment can both persuade the agency and provide grounds for legal challenge if the rule is finalized without addressing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show how unique personal or stakeholder situations affect behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that reflect the perspective of individual persons can show unique situations the agency hasn’t contemplated and explain how those situations will impact individual behavior in response to the policy change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe specific behavioral responses and practical impacts rather than only abstract opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear citations to rule text when responding to specific items
rubrics_metrics.description: When responding to a particular word or phrase or to specific questions, state this clearly and provide the relevant page number, column, and paragraph citation from the Federal Register document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pinpointing exact language helps the agency locate and consider your point; reference the preamble or regulatory text precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit comments on time and to the proper docket
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit your comment during the comment window identified in the preamble and place it in the correct docket folder on regulations.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Register preamble identifies the deadline. Use the docket folder (linked from the Federal Register) and the 'Comment Now!' or 'Submit a formal comment' functions; timely and properly filed comments will be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know where to find proposed rules and notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Federal Register (federalregister.gov) to find notices and proposed rules (NPRMs) and to get the docket number and preamble information you'll need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filter by proposed rules or notices, search by keyword, RIN, or agency name; read the full proposal and the preamble to find the comment deadline and in-notice prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use regulations.gov to file and attach supporting materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov is the official site for public comments; each rule has a docket folder containing the proposed rule, supporting documents, and public comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can type your comment into the provided text box or upload a file. Two submission routes: 'Submit a formal comment' from the Federal Register page or search the docket on regulations.gov and click 'Comment Now!'.
